binary-search.pattern: Classic binary search on a sorted array (halve the range each step)

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Check every element from the left until `target` is found.
steps: For each index `i`, if `nums[i] == target`, return `i`.
Return −1 if the scan finishes.
approaches.why: It may look at all n elements; it ignores that the array is sorted, and the problem asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Binary search
approaches.idea: Compare `target` with the middle element: if they are equal you are done; if `target` is larger it can only be in the right half, otherwise only in the left half. Each comparison halves the range.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = n − 1`.
While `lo <= hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
If `nums[mid] == target`, return `mid`; if `nums[mid] < target`, set `lo = mid + 1`; else `hi = mid − 1`.
Return −1 when the range is empty.
approaches.why: The range halves every step, so at most about log₂ n + 1 steps. `lo + (hi − lo) / 2` avoids the overflow that `(lo + hi) / 2` can cause for huge ranges.

search-insert-position.pattern: Lower bound: the first index whose value is ≥ target

approaches.name: Linear scan for the first value ≥ target
approaches.idea: The answer is the first position whose value is at least `target` — that is where `target` is or would go. Scan for it.
steps: For each `i`, if `nums[i] >= target`, return `i`.
If no value is that large, return `n` (insert at the end).
approaches.why: It may scan the whole array; the problem asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Binary search for the lower bound
approaches.idea: Search over positions `0..n` (n means "after the end"). If `nums[mid] < target` the answer is to the right of `mid`; otherwise `mid` itself could be the answer, so keep it in range.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = n`.
While `lo < hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`; if `nums[mid] < target`, `lo = mid + 1`, else `hi = mid`.
Return `lo` (where `lo == hi`).
approaches.why: The half-open range `[lo, hi)` shrinks by half each step and always contains the answer, so the loop ends on it.

first-bad-version.pattern: Binary search on a monotone yes/no predicate (first true)

approaches.name: Try every version from 1
approaches.idea: Call `isBadVersion(1)`, `isBadVersion(2)`, … and return the first version that is bad.
steps: For `v` from 1 to `n`, if `isBadVersion(v)` is true, return `v`.
(A bad version is guaranteed, so the loop always returns.)
approaches.why: Up to n API calls. With n near 2³¹ that is billions of calls.

approaches.name: Binary search for the first bad version
approaches.idea: The versions look like good, good, …, good, bad, …, bad. If `mid` is bad, the first bad version is `mid` or earlier; if it is good, the first bad one is after `mid`.
steps: Set `lo = 1`, `hi = n`.
While `lo < hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
If `isBadVersion(mid)`, set `hi = mid`; otherwise `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About 31 calls for n up to 2³¹ − 1. Writing `(lo + hi) / 2` would overflow a 32-bit int here, which is the classic bug this problem tests.

sqrtx.pattern: Binary search on the answer (largest r with r² ≤ x)

approaches.name: Count up while the square fits
approaches.idea: Try r = 1, 2, 3, … while `(r + 1)²` is still at most `x`.
steps: Set `r = 0`.
While `(r + 1) × (r + 1) <= x` (computed in 64 bits), increase `r`.
Return `r`.
approaches.why: About √x steps — up to 46,341 for the largest input, which is acceptable but grows with x.

approaches.name: Binary search on r
approaches.idea: Whether `r² <= x` is true for small r and false from some point on. Binary search for the last r where it is true.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = x` (for `x >= 1` the answer is at most x).
While `lo < hi`: take the upper middle `mid = lo + (hi − lo + 1) / 2`.
If `mid × mid <= x` (64-bit), set `lo = mid`; otherwise `hi = mid − 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: About 31 steps. The upper middle is needed because `lo = mid` would otherwise loop forever when `hi = lo + 1`.

approaches.name: Newton's method on integers
approaches.idea: Newton's iteration `r ← (r + x / r) / 2` converges to √x very fast. Starting from `r = x` and using integer division, the values decrease until `r² <= x`; that r is the floor of the square root.
steps: Set `r = x`.
While `r × r > x` (64-bit), set `r = (r + x / r) / 2` with integer division.
Return `r`.
approaches.why: From a far-away start each step roughly halves r; near the root the number of correct digits doubles each step. In practice under 20 iterations for 32-bit x.

find-first-and-last-position-of-element-.pattern: Two binary searches: lower bound (first ≥ target) and upper bound (first > target)

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Walk the array and record the first and last index where `target` appears.
steps: Set `first = last = −1`.
For each `i` with `nums[i] == target`: if `first == −1`, set `first = i`; always set `last = i`.
Return `[first, last]`.
approaches.why: One full pass; the problem requires O(log n).

approaches.name: Binary search once, then expand
approaches.idea: Find any position of `target` with binary search, then walk left and right while the neighbours are still `target`.
steps: Binary search for any index `p` with `nums[p] == target`; if none, return `[−1, −1]`.
Move `l` left from `p` while `nums[l − 1] == target`, and `r` right while `nums[r + 1] == target`.
Return `[l, r]`.
approaches.why: k is the number of copies of `target`. If the whole array is `target`, k = n and this degrades to O(n).

approaches.name: Lower bound and upper bound
approaches.idea: The first occurrence is the first index with value `>= target`; one past the last occurrence is the first index with value `> target`. Both are plain binary searches.
steps: Write `firstAtLeast(v)`: the smallest index with `nums[i] >= v` (or n).
`start = firstAtLeast(target)`. If `start == n` or `nums[start] != target`, return `[−1, −1]`.
`end = firstAtLeast(target + 1) − 1` (values are integers, so "> target" is "≥ target + 1").
Return `[start, end]`.
approaches.why: Two binary searches regardless of how many copies there are. `target + 1` fits: targets are at most 10⁹.

search-a-2d-matrix.pattern: Binary search over a matrix read as one sorted array (index → row, column)

approaches.name: Check every cell
approaches.idea: Scan all m × n cells for `target`.
steps: For each row and each column, if the cell equals `target`, return true.
Return false after the scan.
approaches.why: Every cell may be checked; the sorted order is ignored.

approaches.name: Staircase walk from the top-right corner
approaches.idea: At the top-right cell, everything to the left is smaller and everything below is larger. If the cell is too big, drop its column; if too small, drop its row.
steps: Start at row 0, column n − 1.
If the cell equals `target`, return true.
If it is greater than `target`, move left; otherwise move down.
Return false when you leave the matrix.
approaches.why: Each step removes a row or a column. This works even when only rows and columns are sorted separately; here the stronger ordering allows O(log(m·n)).

approaches.name: One binary search over m·n positions
approaches.idea: Because each row starts after the previous row ends, reading the rows one after another gives one sorted array of length m·n. Position `k` of it is cell `(k / n, k % n)`.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = m·n − 1`.
While `lo <= hi`: `mid` is the middle; its value is `matrix[mid / n][mid % n]`.
Return true on a match; otherwise move `lo` or `hi` past `mid` as in normal binary search.
Return false.
approaches.why: A single binary search over m·n positions, with O(1) index arithmetic per step.

find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.pattern: Binary search comparing the middle with the right end (which half holds the drop)

approaches.name: Scan for the smallest value
approaches.idea: Look at every value and keep the smallest. (Equivalently, find the one place where a value is smaller than the one before it.)
steps: Set `best = nums[0]`.
For each value, update `best` if it is smaller.
Return `best`.
approaches.why: One full pass; the problem asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Binary search against the last element
approaches.idea: If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the drop (and the minimum) lies to the right of `mid`. Otherwise the part from `mid` to `hi` is sorted, so the minimum is at `mid` or to its left.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = n − 1`.
While `lo < hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, set `lo = mid + 1`; else set `hi = mid`.
Return `nums[lo]`.
approaches.why: The range halves every step. Comparing with `nums[hi]` (not `nums[lo]`) also handles an array that is not rotated at all. Distinct values make the comparison decisive.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.pattern: Modified binary search: one half around mid is always sorted

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.idea: Check every index for `target`.
steps: For each `i`, if `nums[i] == target`, return `i`.
Return −1.
approaches.why: It may look at every element; the problem asks for O(log n).

approaches.name: Find the rotation point, then binary search one run
approaches.idea: First find the index of the minimum (the start of the second sorted run) with binary search. Then `target` can only be in one of the two sorted runs; binary search that one.
steps: Find `p`, the index of the minimum, as in "Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array".
If `target` is between `nums[p]` and `nums[n − 1]`, search `[p, n − 1]`; otherwise search `[0, p − 1]`.
Run an ordinary binary search on that range.
approaches.why: Two binary searches. Same complexity as the one-pass version, just a little more code.

approaches.name: One binary search, deciding which half is sorted
approaches.idea: Around any `mid`, at least one of the halves `[lo, mid]` and `[mid, hi]` is sorted. Check whether `target` lies within the sorted half's range; if so search there, otherwise search the other half.
steps: While `lo <= hi`: compute `mid`; if `nums[mid] == target`, return `mid`.
If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` (left half sorted): if `nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]`, set `hi = mid − 1`, else `lo = mid + 1`.
Otherwise (right half sorted): if `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]`, set `lo = mid + 1`, else `hi = mid − 1`.
Return −1.
approaches.why: Each step discards half of the range, as in plain binary search. The `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` matters when `lo == mid`.

find-peak-element.pattern: Binary search on the slope (always climb towards the higher neighbour)

approaches.name: Find the first downward step
approaches.idea: Walking from the left, the values rise until the first time they fall; the element just before that fall is a peak. If they never fall, the last element is a peak.
steps: For each `i` from 0 to n − 2: if `nums[i] > nums[i + 1]`, return `i`.
Return `n − 1`.
approaches.why: One pass. It is correct because everything before the first fall was rising, so `nums[i] > nums[i − 1]` too.

approaches.name: Binary search towards the rising side
approaches.idea: If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, the values climb to the right, and since the edge counts as −∞ there must be a peak to the right. Otherwise `mid` is on a downhill (or is a peak), so a peak exists at `mid` or to its left.
steps: Set `lo = 0`, `hi = n − 1`.
While `lo < hi`: `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`.
If `nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]`, set `lo = mid + 1`; else set `hi = mid`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: The range halves every step and always contains a peak. `mid + 1` is safe because `mid < hi` inside the loop.

median-of-two-sorted-arrays.pattern: Binary search on the partition of the shorter array

approaches.name: Concatenate and sort
approaches.idea: Put all values in one array, sort it, and read the middle.
steps: Copy both arrays into one array of length m + n and sort it.
If the length is odd, return the middle value; otherwise the average of the two middle values.
approaches.why: The sort dominates and ignores that both inputs are already sorted.

approaches.name: Merge walk up to the middle
approaches.idea: Like the merge step of merge sort, take the smaller front value of the two arrays each time — but stop once the middle position is reached, remembering the last two values taken.
steps: Let `t = m + n`. Walk `i` over `nums1` and `j` over `nums2`, each step taking the smaller front value (or the only one left).
Track the previous and current values taken; stop after taking `t / 2 + 1` values.
Return the current value if `t` is odd, else the average of previous and current.
approaches.why: About (m + n)/2 steps and two remembered values; no merged array is built.

approaches.name: Binary search the cut in the shorter array
approaches.idea: Cut both arrays so the left parts together hold `half = (m + n + 1) / 2` values. Taking `i` from the shorter array fixes `j = half − i` from the other. The cut is right when every left value is ≤ every right value: `A[i − 1] <= B[j]` and `B[j − 1] <= A[i]`. Binary search `i`.
steps: Make `A` the shorter array (length m). Search `i` in `[0, m]`, with `j = half − i`.
Read the four border values, using −∞/+∞ when a side is empty.
If `Aleft > Bright`, move `i` left (`hi = i − 1`); if `Bleft > Aright`, move `i` right (`lo = i + 1`).
Otherwise the cut is correct: the median is `max(Aleft, Bleft)` for an odd total, or the average of that and `min(Aright, Bright)` for an even total.
approaches.why: The binary search runs over the m + 1 possible cuts of the shorter array; each step is O(1). Searching the shorter array also guarantees `j` stays within `[0, n]`.
